THOUGHT: The patient is a 38-year-old woman with a solitary, painless, nonpruritic, slowly enlarging skin lesion on the right thigh for one month. Key clinical features include: (1) hyperpigmented papule measuring 0.8 cm; (2) positive “dimple sign” — inward retraction upon lateral compression, which reflects tethering of the lesion to the underlying dermis due to fibrous proliferation; (3) absence of inflammation (no erythema, warmth, or discharge); (4) no systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, weight loss, night sweats), making systemic or infectious etiologies unlikely; (5) dermoscopic findings — central white patch (representing dense collagen/fibrosis) and peripheral pigment network (reflecting melanin-laden macrophages and preserved epidermal rete pattern) — classic for dermatofibroma; and (6) histopathology confirming benign fibroblastic proliferation, i.e., dermatofibroma. While other entities such as melanocytic nevus, basal cell carcinoma, or cutaneous metastasis could present as pigmented papules, the dimple sign, lack of growth acceleration, absence of atypical dermoscopic features (e.g., blue-white veil, irregular streaks, regression structures), and definitive histopathologic confirmation all strongly support dermatofibroma as the diagnosis. Dermatofibromas are common, benign, fibrous histiocytomas typically occurring in young to middle-aged adults, often on the lower extremities, and frequently associated with minor trauma (though not always recalled).

DIAGNOSIS: Dermatofibroma
